In the context of reinforcement learning, off-policy evaluation in confounded settings is a significant problem that has been addressed by developing marginal importance weights as a framework for assessing policies.  This method is advantageous because it can be applied to a wide range of environments, including those with multiple states and actions.  Nevertheless, calculating the optimal policy using marginal importance weights is computationally challenging due to the need to repeatedly solve a complex value iteration problem.  This paper proposes a new approach to solving this challenge, specifically focusing on the issue of finding the optimal policy with the highest expected return.  This approach involves transforming the value iteration problem into a more manageable optimization task, and we show that it is possible to solve this problem using a gradient-based method.  We also demonstrate the potential for further acceleration through the application of Newton's method, and finally, we validate the practical effectiveness of our approach using numerical experiments.  These experiments show that our proposed method is capable of outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods.  Additionally, we explore the application of our method to a more general setting involving multiple policies, and we provide an algorithm for this more general scenario as well.  We also offer an open-source implementation of our methods.  This implementation can be accessed at the following GitHub repository: https://github.com/bernd-lepelken/miw. Training neural networks on long temporal data is a computationally expensive task, especially when using backpropagation, which requires recalculating weights backward.  An alternative method, known as Skip-Sideways, was proposed to address this issue.  Unlike traditional methods that utilize a gradient descent algorithm to update weights, Skip-Sideways uses a queue-based approach to apply gradients in a forward manner, eliminating the need to recalculate weights.  Our study aimed to validate the Skip-Sideways approach by comparing its performance with other methods, focusing on both its computational efficiency and effectiveness.  We conducted an in-depth analysis of Skip-Sideways, examining its training dynamics and efficiency, and then applied it to real-world datasets, evaluating its accuracy in comparison to other state-of-the-art models.  Our results indicate that Skip-Sideways not only reduces training time but also achieves comparable accuracy to its counterparts.  Furthermore, our analysis of training dynamics suggests that Skip-Sideways successfully adapts to temporal data while maintaining a stable performance.  Overall, our findings support the potential of Skip-Sideways as a viable alternative for training neural networks on temporal data.  The Skip-Sideways code is available for public access at https://github.com/asharkhawaja/skip_sideways.  We also propose a new method, Skip-Sideways-Res, which combines Skip-Sideways with residual connections to further enhance its performance.  Our analysis of this method's performance shows that it outperforms Skip-Sideways, achieving superior accuracy while maintaining computational efficiency.  We anticipate that our research will inspire further exploration of efficient training methods for temporal data.  Our proposed approach may also be applied to other areas of research, such as reinforcement learning and time-series forecasting.  The potential applications of this research are vast and promising, with the possibility of extending it to other fields, including reinforcement learning and time-series forecasting.  The full text of this research is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.11944.  We also provide a comprehensive overview of our research findings in a related video at https://youtu.be/6Qh6Qh6Qh6Q.  The corresponding author can be reached via email at a.sharkhawaja@uwe.ac.uk. The widespread adoption of multimodal interfaces in our daily interactions has generated substantial interest in the database community, particularly in developing comprehensive query languages that can effectively manage complex multimodal data. Currently, existing query languages are limited in their ability to consider implicit relationships between different modalities, often neglecting issues like sentiment analysis and user intent. In contrast, relational databases have a long history of using primary-secondary relationship definitions to enhance query processing efficiency. Building upon this concept, we propose a novel approach to defining relationships between multimodal data, enabling the efficient evaluation of complex queries. Specifically, we introduce the concept of "multimodal link definitions" to formally define relationships between modalities, allowing for the creation of "multimodal primary and secondary link definitions." We then develop a framework for evaluating multimodal queries based on these definitions, along with a proof of its correctness and an implementation of a query engine that supports "multimodal primary and secondary link definitions." Furthermore, we conduct an experimental evaluation of our query engine on real-world multimodal data, demonstrating its effectiveness in processing complex queries efficiently. The results show that our approach can significantly reduce query processing time, with an average speedup of 2.7-3.5 times, compared to traditional query languages. We also demonstrate the scalability of our method by processing large multimodal datasets containing over 100,000 records. To optimize deep learning models for deployment on resource-constrained mobile devices, researchers employ model pruning. However, this approach is limited by its reliance on pre-training models, making it unsuitable for applications with limited data or those where data-driven optimization is crucial. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach to model pruning, leveraging a self-supervised training method that simultaneously optimizes both network architecture and feature extraction. By utilizing a contrastive loss function, we identify the most critical features for classification and prune corresponding layers, with the pruning process being driven by data-driven optimization. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, achieving comparable performance to state-of-the-art methods on benchmark datasets. Furthermore, our approach enables the creation of more efficient models that can match or outperform existing solutions. Code is available at https://github.com/tclt/corr_pruning. The exponential growth of scholarly publications has heightened the necessity for a systematic literature review, but the overwhelming nature of these publications has made it increasingly difficult for researchers to identify relevant and reliable information. To address this issue, we propose a collaborative approach that involves users actively participating in the development of a recommendation system. By combining user input with a query-based ranking method, our system can effectively guide users to the most relevant publications. The query-based ranking method utilizes a unique query feature extraction technique, combining the user's search query with the collective queries of peers who have viewed the same publications, and then integrates this information with the user's interaction data to enhance the ranking accuracy. The results of our experiments demonstrate that our collaborative approach significantly improves the performance of information retrieval systems. Furthermore, our study also reveals that the recommendations generated by our system align well with the user ratings provided in the literature reviews. The outcomes of our research indicate that our collaborative approach can be a valuable tool for supporting literature review and recommendation. Recent studies have demonstrated that self-supervised learning methods can mitigate the catastrophic forgetting problem when pre-trained on unlabeled data and applied to a new, limited unlabeled dataset in comparison to fully supervised methods. Nevertheless, the pre-training process employed in these studies may be hindering the full potential of self-supervised methods. In this research, we investigate the influence of the pre-training process on the forgetting rate and discover that the widely-used approach of pre-training a model on a large dataset and fine-tuning it on a small dataset using a single task is not the most effective. Our findings suggest that the smoothing effect observed in self-supervised methods is primarily a consequence of using a single task and a single pre-training method. By employing a more comprehensive approach, involving the use of multiple tasks and diverse pre-training methods, we observe a significant reduction in the forgetting rate. Our research implies that the current smoothing effect observed in self-supervised methods is not solely due to the inherent properties of these methods, but rather a result of their limitations. Moreover, our work introduces a novel self-supervised framework known as the Smooth Framework, which integrates the strengths of self-supervised and fully supervised methods. By combining the two approaches, the framework enables the creation of a more comprehensive representation manifold, leading to improved performance on out-of-distribution tasks. Our results demonstrate the potential of the proposed framework in addressing catastrophic forgetting and enhancing the generalizability of deep neural networks. Complex systems such as weather forecasting, traffic, and supply chain management yield extensive amounts of spatial-temporal data. Historically, analyzing these data sets required either high-resolution models that consumed excessive computational resources or low-resolution models that compromised accuracy. Machine learning methods like CNNs have been employed to tackle this challenge, but they are often limited to either spatial or temporal data, ignoring the inherent correlations between space and time. A novel CNN architecture presented in this research addresses this issue by incorporating both spatial and temporal filters to provide accurate, efficient predictions for complex dynamic systems. The proposed model's effectiveness is demonstrated through numerical simulations of traffic flow prediction, highlighting its superiority over spatial-temporally separate CNN architectures. Furthermore, experiments on large-scale traffic flow prediction showcase the model's scalability and efficiency. The proposed architecture is expected to facilitate the application of machine learning methods to a broad spectrum of spatially and temporally correlated dynamic systems. A silicon-based material is examined for its susceptibility to laser-induced damage.  When subjected to laser pulses, silicon undergoes thermal shock, causing melting and subsequent thermal emission that depends on the laser's power and duration.  By analyzing thermal emission spectra, it is possible to determine the critical temperature of melting and the cooling rate of the melt front.  By varying the laser's power and duration, it is possible to control the level of damage inflicted on silicon samples.  High-powered lasers can create nanoscale craters through ablation, while lower-powered lasers primarily cause melting.  The observed melting and ablation phenomena are similar to those reported in silicon substrates used for solar cells. By analyzing the defect density and comparing it to the thermal shock parameters, it is possible to determine the critical temperature and cooling rate of melting.  The observed damage mechanisms are further supported by numerical simulations of laser-induced thermal shock and material damage. To mitigate its performance issues with long-lasting water waves, we employ a novel reformulation of the advection term within the continuous advection-adiabatic FLIP framework. This reformulation relies on a local estimate of the advection field derived from the previous fluid velocity estimate. Our approach is validated through various experiments, including the simulation of a drop falling onto a dry surface, a drop falling onto water, a sphere falling into water, a high-speed object penetrating water, and the simulation of complex scenes with multiple splashes. Our findings demonstrate that the reformulated advection scheme effectively minimizes the accumulation of errors associated with the standard scheme. Furthermore, we explore the potential of combining this reformulated advection method with the standard velocity update scheme in a hybrid approach. Our experiments reveal that this hybrid strategy can be more effective than solely using the reformulated advection scheme, although it may not always result in the optimal balance between accuracy and efficiency. Overall, our research presents a new approach to modeling water splashes, enabling the efficient and accurate simulation of complex scenarios. methods in predicting missing links and classifying network nodes. The code for

In this study, we introduce a novel approach, Feature Alignment via Clustering (FAC), which leverages this camera cluster information to enhance feature alignment. By dividing images into clusters based on camera proximity, FAC aligns features at the cluster level, resulting in improved performance. Our proposed method is flexible and can be easily integrated into existing person re-reidentification systems. Experimental results demonstrate that FAC outperforms existing methods, with notable improvements in ranking accuracy and retrieval precision, achieving a significant 4.4% increase over the state-of-the-art method when using a single GPU and 6.9% when using multiple GPUs. The traditional DQN algorithm is susceptible to the limitations of its learned Q-function, which can fail to accurately estimate the optimal action. To overcome this issue, we introduce a novel algorithm that simultaneously trains a Q-function and an ensemble of deterministic action generators. These action generators learn to produce diverse scenarios, each representing different possible outcomes of taking an action as opposed to a single predicted outcome derived from the Q-function. By leveraging these diverse scenarios, we can effectively assess the potential risks associated with taking a particular action. Our proposed algorithm, DQFEnsemble, integrates the Q-function with the action generators to provide a more comprehensive and accurate estimation of the optimal action. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we conducted experiments on the Cartpole and AirLift environments, and the results show that DQFEnsemble outperforms the original DQN algorithm in both accuracy and efficiency. Furthermore, we applied DQFEnsemble to the AirLift environment to create a more informed and diverse exploration strategy, and the outcome was a significant increase in the number of episodes required to solve the environment. Our findings suggest that training deterministic action generators in conjunction with the Q-function can lead to a more effective and efficient approach to reinforcement learning. Secure end-to-end encryption has become a standard in online communication, but this comes at the cost of complex functionality for clients. This has led to the development of client-side protocols that can detect suspicious activity, but these often compromise users' anonymity by requiring clients to store and process plaintext. This paper proposes Wink, a system that allows clients to send covert messages, enabling them to detect suspicious activity, self-report to the server, and keep user communications private. Wink achieves this by adding secret signals to the public part of encrypted messages, making it nearly undetectable for attackers to identify these covert messages, even with access to the encrypted text. Wink's design ensures that a user's communications remain and appear normal in normal use scenarios, but reveal the secret signals to the attacker when the user suspects a server or network compromise. We have developed Wink's implementation using the Signal protocol and tested its security and performance on modern devices. Our results show that Wink allows clients to detect and self-report suspicious activity, even in cases where the server is attempting to detect and self-report the secret signals. This research demonstrates the feasibility of a client-side secure messaging system that balances privacy, detectability, and usability. We have also evaluated the limitations and potential vulnerabilities of Wink, highlighting the need for further research in this area. In contrast, we introduce a point-voxel representation that leverages the efficiency of deep learning for processing 3D data, by mapping each voxel to a point and representing spatial relationships through learned voxel sizes. This representation enables the use of simple, lightweight networks that can efficiently process point-level data, leading to faster inference times and improved scalability. A common issue with machine learning models is their susceptibility to noise, which can lead to subpar performance. While data preprocessing methods are often used to address this, they don't always work for complex noise scenarios. This paper explores the application of a robust learning theory framework to improve the resilience of deep learning models of any architecture. We introduce the idea of a "learnability lock," a secure container for machine learning models that ensures the model's integrity by only allowing it to be used within specified secure conditions. This concept is realized through a novel technique called "lockable neural networks," where we integrate a neural network with a secure module that governs the model's application according to predefined security protocols. This approach maintains the efficiency of the neural network's original architecture, preserving its ability to learn and reason. Our research focuses on developing a robust learnability lock that effectively safeguards against various attacks, including data tampering and model extraction threats, while ensuring the model remains functional. This secure approach is demonstrated through experiments with MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets. This work is part of an ongoing effort to develop a comprehensive framework for secure machine learning models. High-dimensional statistics and machine learning heavily rely on a crucial result known as Wedin's $\sin$ $\theta$ theorem. This research introduces a groundbreaking spiking neural network that utilizes local synaptic learning rules to identify and track individuals walking, even in cluttered environments. Our innovative network is comprised of two layers of neurons, where the first layer processes input from a sophisticated feature extraction algorithm and translates it into spikes, and the second layer leverages these spikes to recognize and track walking individuals. We provide a comprehensive and detailed description of the blocks within the representation category of any reductive algebraic group, specifically those defined over fields of a positive characteristic, by treating them as a self-contained algebraic structure, known as a local algebras or local categories. These blocks are characterized by their unique properties, including being local algebras and categories, as well as having specific dimensions, degrees, and decomposition numbers that are entirely controlled by the group's formal structure, known as the fibration class. This work extends previous findings in the field, where similar descriptions were achieved for groups over a field of characteristic zero, and also presents a new, unified approach to the blocks of finite groups, which was previously developed by R. Dipper and H. H. Weyl. Additionally, we demonstrate that the blocks of reductive groups are invariant under automorphisms of the group, a result that is also applicable to finite groups, as shown by R. Dipper and H. H. Weyl. Furthermore, we apply these findings to the group of linear transformations to confirm a conjecture by J. B. Thévenaz and D. A. Vogan that the blocks of this group are controlled by the group's formal structure, known as the fibration class. This work also includes a detailed description of the blocks of this group, which is a key step towards understanding the representation theory of the group of linear transformations to an $n$-dimensional vector space. Finally, we provide a self-contained proof of the block decomposition theorem for finite groups, which was previously developed by R. Dipper and H. H. Weyl. Deep learning models excel in tasks such as image classification and object detection when trained on large datasets, but they often struggle to generalize to new datasets with different characteristics. This problem is particularly challenging when datasets are small, as seen in the case of single-image super-resolution. Our research reveals that one of the main reasons for this difficulty lies in the difference in distribution between the training and testing datasets. To overcome this challenge, we propose a novel approach that utilizes a dataset-specific weight adjustment mechanism for the intermediate layers of pre-trained networks. Our method, known as DOWA, outperforms existing techniques by a significant margin, as measured by the PSNR and SSIM metrics in single-image super-resolution. Furthermore, we show that our dataset-dependent approach allows for more efficient utilization of limited data resources. To our knowledge, this study is the first to explore dataset-driven pre-training in the context of single-image super-resolution. Machinery malfunctions can be identified by analyzing the fluctuations in the machinery's operational parameters over time. Conventional machine learning methods rely on a set of predefined features, which may not accurately capture the complex nature of the malfunction. This paper introduces the temporal logic neural network (TLNN), a novel deep learning approach that extracts relevant features from raw data and learns a logic-based representation to improve diagnostic accuracy. Compared to conventional methods, TLNN exhibits superior performance and robustness against noisy data, yielding a 99.64% diagnostic accuracy rate in experiments with common window-based diagnostic datasets. TLNN's underlying logic-based representation enables the detection of complex malfunctions that conventional approaches cannot, making it a more interpretable diagnostic tool. Additionally, TLNN's ability to learn a logic-based representation enables it to generate a diagnostic explanation in a human-readable format, further solidifying its utility in machinery diagnosis. Inductive logic programming systems have been gaining more attention due to their potential in learning logic rules from data, but they often struggle with generating accurate rules that apply universally. To overcome this limitation, a new system called ILP-Net has been developed, utilizing a neural network framework that combines a teacher network with an experience replay network. The teacher network applies existing rules to user-provided data, generating partial results, which are then fed into the experience replay network to generate new rules. This system employs a novel approach known as contrastively enhanced self-supervised learning to learn from these additional results, effectively producing more comprehensive and accurate rules. Through various benchmark tests, ILP-Net has demonstrated its superiority over other state-of-the-art systems, achieving significant improvements in certain domains by as much as 50%. This achievement underscores the potential of ILP systems to learn from data, and ILP-Net has the potential to become a valuable tool in this field. However, the existing GAN models fail to produce photorealistic 3D facial textures effectively. To address this limitation, a novel approach called DeepFaceText (DFT) is introduced, which employs a GAN framework to synthesize realistic facial textures. These vulnerabilities pose significant risks to safety-critical systems, such as self-driving cars. To combat this issue, we introduce an innovative defense mechanism that leverages the concept of adversarial perturbations to generate robust features for neural networks. By combining these robust features with additional information, such as spatial data, from the input image, our model can effectively detect and correct adversarial attacks. Notably, our model exhibits comparable or improved performance compared to existing methods without adversarial training for image classification tasks. Furthermore, our model can be integrated with existing detection methods to enhance their robustness against adversarial attacks. The problem of identifying quantum states can be related to determining the presence of perfect matching under specific vertex-color constraints, which can be further classified into two sub-problems, generalized perfect matching and exact perfect matching. We propose a quantum algorithm that solves generalized perfect matching on a complete graph with n vertices and m edges in O(n) time, significantly outperforming the previously known O(m) time limit. Additionally, we establish a quantum algorithm that solves exact perfect matching on a complete bipartite graph with n vertices and m edges in O(m/sqrt(m)) time, surpassing the previously known O(m) time limit. These advancements are made possible by a novel quantum algorithm that solves the problem of state identification in the Grover-Hadamard model in O(n) and O(m) time, respectively. We also show that solving state identification in O(m) time would resolve one of the open problems in the field of quantum algorithm design. Our results show that our method outperforms existing approaches in estimating the asymptotic variance, particularly in moderate to large sample sizes. Moreover, our derived error bound provides a useful metric to assess the impact of dependencies on control of the false discovery rate. The method is also applicable in scenarios where the covariance matrix is unknown and needs to be estimated. In the context of hypergraph matching Ramsey numbers, we are tasked with finding the largest possible size of a vertex set that contains no non-trivial matches – i.e., matches with at least one pair of vertices shared by both sets – within a k-uniform hypergraph with n vertices. This concept is an extension of the traditional graph matching Ramsey number, R(H, k), where H is a two-part set consisting of two identical vertices. This work focuses on determining the R(3, r) hypergraph matching Ramsey number for any given non-negative integer r, particularly when r is 9 or more, in which case we establish a lower and upper bound of at least 5 times 4 to the power of r, plus 7 and at most 7 times 4 to the power of r, respectively. This bound is significant as it provides a definitive answer to the long-standing problem posed by Sheehan and Luczak in 2015 for the specific case of r = 9. The research further explores the R(3, r) problem for certain graph classes with specific properties. Specifically, for r = 9, it is proven that the R(3, r) problem can be solved in linear time for triangle-free graphs and in O(n^3) time for triangle-critical graphs. This work also provides a characterization of the R(3, r) problem for r = 9 and 10 for triangle-critical graphs. Lastly, for r = 9 and 10, it is proven that the R(3, r) problem can be solved in linear time for triangle-free graphs with a girth of 5 or more. This work further extends the existing literature on the R(3, r) problem for r = 9 and 10. A key challenge in developing effective feedback control policies via modern machine learning methods is collecting and labeling feedback data, a task that is often impractical or costly. To address this issue, we introduce a novel self-supervised algorithm that enables learning of feedback control policies directly from raw state data without requiring experience or labeled feedback. This approach draws inspiration from self-supervised learning in computer vision, where it has achieved impressive results in learning visual representations. To adapt this concept to the control setting, we define a self-supervised loss function that encourages the learned control policy to exhibit stable behavior in response to state inputs. This loss function is derived from the concept of input distribution shift in the state space, a phenomenon that has previously been leveraged in self-supervised learning. Our results demonstrate that this self-supervised algorithm can learn effective feedback control policies for a range of continuous control tasks, including those with high-dimensional state and action spaces, using only raw state data. Furthermore, we show that the learned policies can generalize effectively to unseen states and tasks, even when the training data is limited. This work opens up new possibilities for self-supervised learning of control policies, enabling the development of efficient and scalable methods for learning from raw state data. This paper introduces a cutting-edge image dehazing framework called DHA-Net, which employs a unique combination of a dark knowledge distillation and a new haze estimation method. The framework's architecture consists of a dehazing network and a high-quality haze estimation network. Initially, the dehazing network processes the input image, and its output is used to train the haze estimation network. This process is achieved through a dark knowledge distillation, which leverages the superior performance of the more complex haze estimation network. Our proposed haze estimation method surpasses traditional methods by incorporating a residual learning block and a dense connectivity scheme. These enhancements enable the model to capture intricate features and achieve greater dehazing performance. The future of system-on-chip development lies in 2.5D systems, where multiple
chiplets are interconnected with a silicon interconnect to create a highly
flexible design. However, the widespread adoption of this technology is
complicated by the need to ensure the security of the connected chiplets.
Since each chiplet is unique and manufactured separately, it can be
vulnerable to security threats. This article introduces an innovative security
solution for 2.5D systems, leveraging the interconnect's high degree of freedom
to create a secure connection between the chiplets. The proposed method uses
the silicon interconnect to distribute a secret key, allowing each chiplet to
verify the authenticity of the others. The security of this approach is
validated through an exhaustive mathematical and simulation-based analysis.
The findings demonstrate that this solution provides a secure environment for
the chiplets, even in the face of a substantial number of potential threats. A
practical implementation of the proposed method is also demonstrated using a
field-programmable gate array. The results show that this solution offers a high
degree of security, with a verification accuracy of 99.99%, and a processing
time of less than 1 millisecond for chiplet verification. This research provides
the necessary framework for the secure design and development of future
systems incorporating 2.5D silicon interconnects. The proposed method can be
applied to various applications, including secure 3D chip integration, edge
computing, and IoT device authentication. A comprehensive tutorial on the
design and implementation of the proposed security solution is also provided. 
This article serves as a foundation for researchers and practitioners to design
secure 2.5D systems, and the accompanying software and hardware implementation
are available for reproduction and further study.

Investigating unitary Bose gases following a rapid cooling process, we examine the transition from the Fermi gas to the Bose gas regime. Through Monte Carlo simulations, we analyze the gas' thermodynamic and dynamic properties, focusing on the emergence of closed channel molecules and their statistical distribution. We observe that increasing the gas' density leads to a rise in closed channel molecule production, which can be controlled by adjusting the interaction strength, thereby allowing for a tunable molecular population to reside in both the closed and open channels. Our research reveals that, at unitary criticality, the gas' thermodynamic characteristics are unaffected by the channel population, which is also reflected in the dynamic distribution of closed channel molecules. We compare our results to recent experimental findings and discuss the implications of our findings for understanding the behavior of two-component Fermi gases. Furthermore, we discuss the potential of our cooling protocol to facilitate the creation of a unitary Bose gas featuring a degenerate dark soliton. Notably, the dark soliton's dynamics exhibit distinct behavior in the unitary regime, characterized by a slower decay rate and a larger effective mass compared to that of a free Bose gas. Few-shot learning typically involves a limited number of examples to identify novel categories. Current methods often overlook the differences between old and new knowledge and instead focus on adjusting individual samples to minimize discrepancies. However, this approach can be limited by the fact that old knowledge may already incorporate similar information. In contrast, our method, Few-shot Distillation, focuses on channel-wise adjustments that involve comparing the differences between old and new knowledge more broadly, referred to as 'conceptual' distances. Few-shot Distillation incorporates a 'teacher' network that has a broader scope than the'student' network, allowing the former to have a greater number of parameters. By doing so, our method enables the student to learn from the teacher by emulating the teacher's channel-wise adjustments. Our experiments demonstrate that Few-shot Distillation outperforms existing approaches on various benchmarks, including the miniImageNet, ImageNet, and CIFAR-100 datasets. Our method also generalizes well to unseen classes, further validating its effectiveness. Our code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/THU-DL/Few-shot-Distillation. A crucial technique in wireless communication is Successive Interference Cancellation (SIC), but its performance is compromised when multiple strong signals are present due to the interference cascade effect. Recent advancements in deep learning have enabled the development of more efficient SIC methods, particularly SIC-DNN, which can accurately identify and eliminate strong signals from a single transmission. However, the complexity of the required hardware to support DNN-based SIC systems poses a significant challenge in practical applications. To overcome this limitation, a novel approach called Power-Off DNN (PODNN) has been proposed to reduce the energy consumption of SIC-DNN by selectively disabling the transmitters with the lowest signal quality, thus allowing the remaining transmitters to be processed using the more efficient SIC algorithm. Simulation results demonstrate that PODNN can significantly reduce the required number of hardware resources while maintaining a high detection accuracy, making it an attractive solution for future wireless communication systems. Furthermore, the proposed method can be extended to various SIC algorithms, including Zero-forcing and Minimum Mean Square Error, and is expected to be a key technology in the development of next-generation green and sustainable wireless communication systems. This work also has the potential to be applied to other green communication systems, such as green multiple-input multiple-output, green massive MIMO, and green wireless networks. In offline reinforcement learning, effective policy enhancement relies heavily on the accuracy of learned value functions. Unfortunately, current methods often overlook the primary goal of offline RL - maximizing cumulative rewards, to ensure a stable and smooth value function. To address this limitation, we present a new framework called Stable Value Functions. This approach generates value functions that not only remain stable, but also positive, by leveraging a weighted average of historical policy evaluations. Our theoretical analysis confirms that these value functions are stable and can be effectively used for policy improvement. This innovative program focuses on teaching the principles of data science through hands-on projects that utilize accessible tools and technologies, leading to highly engaging and transformative experiences that yield a wide range of valuable skills and career opportunities for participants. Following the program, many of these individuals went on to secure internships and employment in the tech industry, leading to a significant increase in the number of visually impaired data scientists and consultants who are now working as professionals. This article presents a detailed examination of the program's curriculum, its implementation, and the outcomes of this pioneering initiative. It also highlights the lessons learned and the challenges that need to be considered when designing similar programs for visually impaired individuals, serving as a valuable resource for educators, researchers, and professionals seeking to adapt this approach in their own settings and make data science more accessible to a broader range of participants. To create a lightweight neural network, researchers often rely on time-consuming iterative pruning methods. An alternative approach, weight shifting, reduces the complexity of this process by utilizing a single global parameter. However, this parameter must be carefully adjusted to prevent overfitting and ensure the model's performance remains strong. To address this challenge, we've developed a new method called Iterative Weight Shifting, which iteratively adjusts the weights of a lightweight neural network. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves performance comparable to that of other top models on tasks such as ImageNet and CIFAR-10/100, all while requiring significantly fewer parameters. Furthermore, our technique outperforms other pruning methods in terms of speed and memory efficiency. On a high-end GPU, our method can train and test models at a significantly faster rate, with a speed increase of at least 3.5 times. Additionally, our method can produce a lightweight model that is 3.5 times smaller than the original model, while maintaining its accuracy. To facilitate reproducible research, we've made our code publicly available. Our method can be applied to various types of neural networks, including fully connected, convolutional, and residual networks, and can be easily adapted to other weight-based pruning techniques. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first method to successfully apply iterative pruning techniques to weight shifting. We have also explored the use of weight shifting in conjunction with other pruning methods, which we call hybrid pruning, and have found that this approach can lead to significant performance improvements. Our results demonstrate the potential of weight shifting as a powerful tool for model compression and acceleration. To facilitate the community's research in this area, we've released our code and models on GitHub. In a basic model of voter communication, we examine how echo chambers emerge when voters interact with each other over social media in an unbiased environment. Although initial contact is random, voters with similar views tend to form isolated groups, or echo chambers, due to their reciprocal communication. The size of these echo chambers is influenced by the frequency and quality of in-group conversation as well as the cost of connecting with people who hold differing opinions. By increasing contact with opposing views, such as through the purchase of targeted advertisements, can a minimal communication system be designed that reduces the size of these echo chambers? This novel gradient iterative method is based on reformulating the eigenvalue problem as a minimization problem in which the eigenvalues are minimized while the norm of a matrix's deviation from a diagonal form is minimized, resulting in a well-defined objective function whose gradient can be used to derive an efficient iterative scheme that converges to an approximate solution with fewer than n iterations, resulting in significant computational savings. This approach is particularly beneficial for large-scale eigenvalue problems, which can be solved using a large-scale optimization framework, resulting in a highly efficient and scalable solution method. We demonstrate that PMD-PD achieves a convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}(\frac{\log k}{k})$ for both gap in optimality and constraint violation. We also establish that, under certain conditions, PMD-PD ensures a vanishing constraint violation, even in the absence of certain assumptions. To further enhance the algorithm, we introduce a strategy for warm-starting, which can significantly reduce computational time when solving similar problems. We validate the algorithm's performance through numerical simulations. The PMD-PD algorithm is part of a broader class of convex optimization methods, and we outline its relationships to other algorithms in this field. Finally, we discuss the potential for extending PMD-PD to nonconvex optimization problems. In the medical domain, collecting patient symptoms is crucial for accurate diagnosis.
Unfortunately, existing methods for collecting symptoms are often flawed due to
their reliance on biased question-probing techniques, which prioritize well-known
symptoms and overlook less common ones. To address this issue, we introduce a
novel approach that employs unsupervised learning to identify symptoms in medical
records. By using a transformer-based model to analyze the language patterns in
these records, we can identify not only the most prevalent symptoms but also
those that are unique to each patient. Through our experiments, we demonstrate
the effectiveness of our method in a real-world setting by implementing it on a
dataset of COVID-19 patients and showing that it can identify a wide range of
symptoms, including those that are less well-known. Moreover, our method outperforms
existing methods by providing more comprehensive and informative results. The code
used in our research is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/IBM/COVID-SymCollect.

In this study, we investigate the robustness of multitask learning in language models and discover that it enhances their ability to function properly even when a significant portion of their neural network is damaged. Our experiments using the GLUE tasks and BERT model indicate that learning multiple tasks at once can improve language representation capabilities when a model is subjected to various forms of neural network failure. These findings suggest that multitask learning may offer a practical solution for mitigating the effects of neural network failures in large language models. In an effort to promote further research, we have made our code and models publicly accessible on GitHub at the following URL: https://github.com/jcyk/robust-mtl. Additionally, we have developed and released a simple web application that allows users to interactively explore the effects of neural network failures in GLUE tasks. This application can be accessed at the following URL: https://mtl-robustness-demo.informatics.indiana.edu/. It is our hope that this study will stimulate further research into the field of robust multitask learning and model robustness in general. We encourage interested readers to share their own discoveries and insights on our discussion forum, located at https://indylabs.github.io/robust-mtl/. Ultimately, we believe that robust multitask learning has the potential to unlock a wide range of innovative applications in natural language processing. We invite readers to explore the many possibilities that this area of research has to offer. The formation of planets within protoplanetary disks is a complex process, particularly due to the presence of a barrier that prevents dust particles from growing in size.  A potential solution to overcome this limitation lies in the collision of dust particles with gas molecules in regions with high gas-to-dust ratios.  By using a combination of numerical simulations and laboratory experiments, we investigated the impact of such collisions on dust particles, discovering that gas-matter collisional growth can significantly contribute to the growth of dust particles in protoplanetary disks, ultimately allowing for the formation of planets in a relatively short period, estimated to be around a few thousand years.  This finding has important implications for the formation of planets in systems with high gas-to-dust ratios.  Furthermore, we propose that gas-matter collisional growth may also be responsible for the formation of hot Jupiter exoplanets.  By using a simplified model, we estimated that gas-matter collisional growth may account for the observed hot Jupiter occurrence rate, provided that the timescale for planet formation is on the order of a few million years.  This finding suggests that the formation of hot Jupiter exoplanets may be closely linked to the growth of dust particles in protoplanetary disks.  A more detailed study of this process is warranted to further understand its underlying mechanisms. In concurrent data structures, locks are an alternative to primitive operations that can be replaced with lock-free operations. However, to release a lock and allow other threads to access the data structure, a reliable method of memory release, or garbage collection, is essential. Three primary techniques for memory release in lock-free algorithms are software-based garbage collection, operating system garbage collection, and kernel garbage collection. Despite their prevalence, there is a lack of comprehensive research on the impact of memory release on lock-free algorithms' performance. This paper conducts an in-depth examination of the effects of memory release on lock-free algorithms' throughput, real-time response, and system-wide resource utilization in Linux-based systems. The study compares the performance of three lock-free algorithms - the atomic linked list, the atomic hash table, and the red-black tree - under different memory release methods, including software-based garbage collection, operating system garbage collection, and kernel garbage collection. The findings reveal that software-based garbage collection has the most significant negative impact on lock-free algorithms' performance, while operating system garbage collection has a moderate negative impact. Kernel garbage collection has the least detrimental effect on lock-free algorithms' performance. The study also shows that the atomic linked list and atomic hash table are more susceptible to performance degradation due to memory release than the red-black tree. These results can serve as a guide for developers to create effective garbage collection techniques for lock-free algorithms and help maintain optimal throughput, real-time response, and system-wide resource utilization. This achievement has sparked significant interest in cross-lingual modeling, which has far-reaching implications for numerous tasks. Our research delves into the cross-lingual characteristics of word embeddings, particularly in relation to semantic relationships within languages. We analyze the cross-lingual properties of word embeddings for languages with varying levels of similarity and dissimilarity – namely English, Italian, and Japanese – by examining the effects of word relationships in one language on another. We investigate whether word embedding models can leverage relationships between words in one language to recognize similar relationships in another language. Our study investigates the cross-lingual effects of various word relationship types, such as synonyms, hypernyms, and others, on different word2vec variants. Our findings indicate that word2vec representations are more susceptible to cross-lingual relationships than GloVe representations, particularly when it comes to synonyms. We also found that different word2vec variants respond differently to cross-lingual relationships, suggesting that the choice of word2vec model is crucial when applying cross-lingual word2vec representations to downstream tasks. Our research provides valuable insights into the characteristics of cross-lingual word2vec representations, which can inform the development of more effective transfer learning models. We also propose a novel approach to cross-lingual word2vec representation learning, based on the idea of "language transfer" and "simultaneous language adaptation". This approach involves learning a word embedding model in a target language by adapting a model in a source language to a new language. Our study demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach in improving the accuracy of word embeddings in a target language. We also explore the potential of this approach in zero-shot learning, where a model is trained on a single language and tested on another language. Our findings suggest that the language transferability of word2vec representations can be significantly improved by using this approach. We also propose a new method for adapting word2vec representations to new languages, which we call "cross-lingual word2vec adaptation". This method involves adapting a pre-trained word2vec model in a source language to a new language, using a transfer learning approach. Our study demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach in improving the accuracy of word2vec representations in a new language, particularly in the context of semantic role labeling. We also investigate the effectiveness of this approach in zero-shot learning, where a model is trained on one language and tested on another.

This research introduces a novel active learning approach for enhancing segmentation in multi-spectral remote sensing images. A key challenge arises from the initial labeling requirements, necessitating a substantial number of labeled pixels, especially in complex scenes. To address this, our method leverages statistical sampling techniques to identify critical pixels for labeling. A segmentation uncertainty metric is first developed to pinpoint areas where labeling would yield the most informative results. Next, a statistical optimization method is employed to determine the optimal number of samples per class. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach yields highly accurate segmentation maps, closely matching those obtained from fully labeled images. Notably, the proposed method requires only a small fraction of labeled pixels to achieve comparable results. For instance, when labeling just 0.5% of the available pixels is sufficient, the method can still produce highly accurate segmentation with an overall accuracy of 95.8%, comparable to fully labeled images (96.0%). Moreover, the proposed method can efficiently identify the most critical pixels to label, thereby minimizing the costs associated with human annotation. Interpolating models that are regularized can achieve strong performance despite their potential for overfitting.  In this study, we investigate the behavior of such models by examining their performance on held-out data.  Our findings suggest that the generalization capacity of interpolating models is not solely dependent on the size of the dataset, nor the level of regularization applied.  To explain our results, we propose a new theory, known as "Implicit Regularization," which posits that the degree of implicit regularization is influenced by the size of the model's weight space relative to the empirical risk minimizer.  To test this theory, we developed a novel "Implicit Generalization Gap" metric that can quantify the degree of implicit regularization in large models.  Our analysis demonstrates that this metric can effectively capture the generalization performance of large models, and can be used to identify the optimal balance between explicit and implicit regularization for optimal performance.  Our results are supported by experiments on large-scale datasets, and we provide evidence that the Implicit Generalization Gap can be used to improve the generalization capacity of such models.  To our knowledge, this study represents the first attempt to quantify the implicit regularization effect in large models. To enhance the efficiency of modern processors, which are often hindered by reordering instructions due to their limited pipeline stages, novel approaches known as promising semantics have been proposed. This approach enables the execution of reordering stages to generate multiple possible outcomes, which are then "promised" to the processor. The results of these outcomes can then be verified once the actual execution is complete, thus allowing the determination of the correct sequence of instructions. This paper introduces a new promising semantics framework that can seamlessly integrate with a wide range of programming languages and processing systems. This framework is founded on the principles of a two-stage verification system, which first generates the promising semantics and then evaluates the accuracy of the results against the traditional program execution sequence. The paper also presents an initial implementation of this framework, which is based on the Racket language, and demonstrates its effectiveness through a series of benchmark tests. The findings suggest that this approach can efficiently verify program correctness, even in scenarios with extensive data manipulation, thus paving the way for its application in a broader range of programming languages. The COVID-19 pandemic has drastically altered daily life and work routines worldwide, with far-reaching consequences for scientific research across various disciplines. This impact extends to the themes under investigation in these fields, including the life sciences. To gain a deeper understanding of the pandemic's influence, a study was conducted to identify the effects of the COVID-19 outbreak on academic research. This involved analyzing nearly 1.2 million research papers from PubMed and Scopus, focusing on publications related to the pandemic, to track changes in their topics and references over time. Our research reveals a notable shift in the types of studies being conducted in response to the pandemic, with an increased focus on human COVID-19, viral transmission, and related topics. Conversely, there has been a decline in the production of cross-species studies. Furthermore, there has been an uptick in the citation of basic research studies, whereas more applied research investigations have seen a decrease. Our findings also indicate that there has been an increase in the use of emerging concepts, such as SARS-CoV-2, COVID-19, and ACE2, yet these terms are often employed in a nonspecific manner. Our research highlights the need for a more structured approach to conducting research on COVID-19, with an emphasis on incorporating existing knowledge from relevant fields. Ultimately, this could help to speed up the pace of scientific discovery and the development of effective treatments for the virus. The primary obstacle in the Structure-from-Motion algorithm is collecting sufficient images with known camera positions. To overcome this challenge, we propose a network that can generate poses for unseen scenes by learning from virtual environments with predictable camera movements, thereby facilitating the construction of a robust Structure-from-Motion pipeline. Our proposed network, called STARS, utilizes a self-supervised learning approach that integrates a 3D reconstruction module to generate synthetic datasets. It then learns to infer camera poses from these datasets without requiring ground truth positions. Our experiments demonstrate that STARS outperforms existing methods in terms of robustness to extreme conditions such as large camera rotations and extreme motion blur. Moreover, our results indicate that STARS can effectively handle scenes with diverse camera positions, achieving comparable results to those from learning from virtual environments. A novel approach to creating stochastic parameterizations involves using machine learning models that can generate realistic patterns of variability from limited data sets. These data sets are typically derived from high-resolution simulations of atmospheric flows under specific conditions. Although promising, this technique has a significant drawback: it requires retraining the models whenever conditions change. To address this issue, we've developed a two-stage training process. First, a GAN model learns patterns of variability from data collected under real-world conditions, and a second model uses this information to simulate patterns of variability under different conditions. By combining these models, we've achieved a stochastic parameterization that can effectively capture real-world patterns of variability, producing results that align well with high-resolution simulations. This innovative approach has the potential to revolutionize our understanding of atmospheric flows under a range of complex conditions. Moreover, it paves the way for the development of more sophisticated parameterizations that can accurately simulate a wide range of environmental scenarios. Building on this success, we adapt the WGAN-GP framework to address the dynamic variant of optimal transport under stochastic dynamics. The original Wasserstein distance metric is modified to accommodate uncertainty in dynamic behavior, and an extended Wasserstein distance is defined accordingly. The results show that our model successfully generates realistic samples from the probability distribution of this stochastic motion, as validated against a ground-truth dataset collected through experimental measurements. Notably, our approach effectively preserves the expected trajectory of the liquid drop under the influence of gravity, thus illustrating its potential for practical applications in optimal control scenarios. The presented work not only extends the original Wasserstein distance to address stochastic dynamics but also offers a practical solution for handling unsteady problems in optimal transport. The proposed approach involves convolving the Lagrangian displacement fields with various Gaussian filters, resulting in a set of Zel'dovich displacement fields that can be used for power spectrum estimation. We also discuss the potential applications of this method to real galaxy surveys and the challenges that need to be addressed in practice. Overall, our method offers a promising approach to improving power spectrum estimation in future galaxy surveys. This research presents near-IR polarization measurements for the first time for certain objects, including a specific brown dwarf, which has never been detected in the optical or near-IR spectra. Analysis revealed that the polarization levels in the H band were lower than expected, with values ranging between 0.5% and 3%. This is attributed to the effects of dust grain size and grain density within the disk systems. Additionally, a specific model of the brown dwarf system GSC 07396-00759 revealed a polarization level of 0.7% and an inclination of approximately 60 degrees, which aligns with previous observations. This research highlights the importance of considering grain size and density when interpreting near-IR polarization data for low-mass objects. Future studies will investigate the properties of other low-mass disks using polarimetric data from the POLISH2 instrument. object detection, as different datasets are often annotated with focus on specific

particular domain, while others concentrate on highlighting certain object parts.

to enhance overall object detection capabilities. Our approach involves merging
annotations from various datasets to create a unified training set, allowing us
to capitalize on the unique strengths of each dataset. We conduct an exhaustive

detection. Our results demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms
training on a single dataset and achieves state-of-the-art performance when
combined with other advanced methods, ultimately leading to improved object
detection capabilities across the board. Furthermore, we contribute a publicly
available tool for merging annotations across diverse datasets, making it an
attractive option for researchers working with multiple datasets. Our project is

We study the stability under perturbation of a time-marginalized stochastic quadruple kernel process. This process generalizes the classical time-marginalized double stochastic process and yields a uniformly elliptic semigroup. We establish a condition, analogous to Foster-Lyapunov's, ensuring the transience of its associated Markov operator. This implies the stability of the semigroup under bounded perturbations. We further investigate the domain of the generator of the perturbed process and obtain a logarithmic H\"older continuity estimate for its transition semigroup. This leads to a logarithmic H\"older continuity estimate for the solution to a related stochastic differential equation. Finally, we apply our findings to a stochastic partial differential equation and derive a logarithmic H\"older continuity estimate for its solution. This result extends previous work by Ferrario and Strainotto to the subcritical case. We achieve our results by combining the Markov selection method with a suitable approximation of the process and leveraging a stochastic integral representation technique. This circumvents the difficulties associated with the stochastic integral of a perturbed process. Instead, we integrate the perturbation into a deterministic process and treat the resulting process with a perturbed process. This approach allows us to study the asymptotic behavior of the process and derive meaningful results. This work is the first to apply the Markov selection method to stochastic partial differential equations. We believe that it opens up new avenues of research in the field. We've developed a new approach to calculating meson decay constants within the framework of an effective mass model. This method involves integrating the wave-packet concept across space and light degrees of freedom, which enables the computation of meson decay constants in a model-independent way. By using the light-front Hamiltonian density, we've derived a well-defined, local wave equation that helps us calculate meson decay constants without encountering singularities. The field of interpretability has gained significant attention in recent years, 
with numerous techniques developed to enhance transparency and explain the 
behaviour of complex models. However, despite the numerous methods proposed, 
there remains a lack of understanding about the stability of model explanations 
when the underlying data is altered, which is particularly crucial in high-stakes 
scenarios. This issue is addressed in this study, which aims to provide a 
comprehensive analysis of the stability of model explanations. Firstly, we 
identify the key factors influencing the stability of model explanations and 
propose a framework based on the components of model explanations to assess 
stability. We then conduct a thorough examination of 14 state-of-the-art 
explanation techniques across 7 datasets, revealing that most methods are 
vulnerable to data variations. This finding highlights the need for further 
research in the area and suggests that future research should focus on 
developing more stable explanation methods, particularly those that can 
withstand data changes. This study also provides valuable insights for model 
developers and practitioners to select suitable explanation methods for their 
specific needs. We release our code and datasets on GitHub to facilitate this 
process. https://github.com/zhuyuezheng/Stability-of-model-explanations.

This paper presents CodeSquirrel, a novel web-based system that employs interactive code analysis to identify code smells directly within integrated development environments, without requiring user-provided code.  CodeSquirrel's core functionality is accessible through a customizable toolbar that integrates seamlessly into popular IDEs like Visual Studio Code, IntelliJ, and Eclipse, allowing for real-time detection of code smells.  Our preliminary evaluation of CodeSquirrel's performance revealed that it accurately identifies 77% of code smells in test cases, with false positives limited to 12.5%.  We further tested CodeSquirrel on real-world projects, yielding promising results, specifically detecting 60% of code smells in the tested projects.  Our study also found CodeSquirrel to be efficient, processing code within code smell detection time, with an average run time of under 1 second.  The comprehensive source code for CodeSquirrel's detection engine is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ahmed-0sama/codesquirrel.  Our research indicates that CodeSquirrel's detection engine is a reliable tool for identifying code smells in real-world applications.  The CodeSquirrel project can be accessed at https://codesquirrel.app.  We anticipate that CodeSquirrel will serve as a valuable resource for developers to identify code smells in real-world applications. In particular, our model achieved a 30% reduction in misclassified pixels compared to the existing YUV444 approach, and a 50% reduction when compared to the best alternative. Gravitational-wave detectors experience irregular disruptions known as glitches, primarily caused by either equipment malfunctions or interactions between high-energy particles and the instruments. These events can interfere with the detection of genuine gravitational waves. In Advanced LIGO, these glitches are analyzed using a method that incorporates machine learning, specifically through a deep neural network. This study focuses on refining the understanding and categorization of these occurrences. This study found that the latter model was more effective in detecting glitch signals. We also discovered that the neural network's ability to accurately classify glitch signals varied based on the specific type of glitch. This research aims to aid in the development of improved glitch identification methods for use in gravitational-wave detectors. Machine learning applications often encounter open set recognition challenges, where novel, unlabelled data appears continuously. To address this issue, a novel approach combining probabilistic latent variable inference and optimization is proposed, allowing models to simultaneously identify known and unknown classes in unlabelled data. This method involves two key components: a posterior inference network and a thresholding objective function. The network maps data to a lower-dimensional space, while the objective function enables the model to identify unknown classes by optimising a threshold value. The proposed method is tested on various datasets and outperforms existing approaches for open set recognition. Additionally, a probabilistic framework is formulated to provide confidence estimates for novel data. Experiments demonstrate that the method produces accurate confidence estimates for both familiar and novel classes. The complete code is made available for reproducibility. High-dimensional time series data is increasingly being analyzed in fields like finance and signal processing using advanced VAR models. However, these models can become impractically complex when dealing with a large number of variables, leading to overfitting issues. This paper introduces a novel Bayesian VAR model specifically designed for high-dimensional time series data that leverages Lasso and L1-penalties to selectively include only the most relevant lag coefficients. Additionally, the proposed model employs Stick-Breaking Priors for sparse prior distributions, allowing for flexible and adaptive prior assignments that can handle high-dimensional data efficiently. Our research presents a Gibbs sampling algorithm for estimating the model's parameters, along with theoretical guarantees for the model's convergence rates. Simulation studies demonstrate the model's effectiveness in identifying sparse VAR models in high-dimensional settings, while real-world applications showcase the practical value of our approach in signal processing. Notably, the proposed model outperforms existing alternatives in terms of out-of-sample predictive accuracy.
